question: What makes an API RESTful, and how do HTTP methods and idempotency work?
reference_answer: REST models resources via nouns in URIs, uses standard HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), communicates statelessly, and returns meaningful status codes. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent—repeating the exact request produces the same server state—whereas POST is generally non-idempotent because repeated calls can create duplicate resources.

question: Explain how React's virtual DOM, state, and reconciliation update the user interface.
reference_answer: React components render a lightweight in-memory tree of elements (Virtual DOM) derived from props and state. When state changes, React diffs the new element tree against the previous one using heuristics (such as element types and list keys) and commits only the minimal DOM mutations needed.
expected_concepts: Virtual DOM|state-driven rendering|reconciliation diffing|list keys|minimal DOM mutations

question: What is CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) and why do browsers enforce it?
reference_answer: Browsers enforce the Same-Origin Policy to stop malicious sites from reading sensitive responses from another origin (scheme, host, port). CORS is a server-controlled opt-in mechanism using headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin and preflight OPTIONS requests to explicitly declare which cross-origin callers, methods, and credentials are allowed.
expected_concepts: Same-Origin Policy|origin scheme host port|Access-Control-Allow-Origin|OPTIONS preflight|browser security

question: Compare session-cookie authentication and JWT Bearer authentication in web apps.
reference_answer: Session cookies store an opaque session ID referencing server-side state, making immediate revocation trivial while requiring CSRF protection (SameSite/CSRF tokens) and shared session storage across servers. Stateless JWTs carry signed claims in the Authorization header, scaling horizontally without DB lookups per request, but require short expiries or denylists for revocation and careful XSS storage hygiene.
expected_concepts: server-side session state|stateless signed claims|revocation trade-off|CSRF vs XSS risks|HttpOnly cookies

question: Explain Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), and how to mitigate each.
reference_answer: XSS injects untrusted scripts into a victim's browser; prevent it with context-aware output escaping, avoiding raw HTML injection, strict Content-Security-Policy (CSP), and HttpOnly cookies. CSRF tricks an authenticated browser into submitting unintended state-changing requests; prevent it with SameSite cookies, anti-CSRF tokens, and Origin/Referer validation.
expected_concepts: XSS script injection|output escaping and CSP|CSRF forged requests|SameSite cookies|anti-CSRF tokens

question: How do HTTP caching headers like Cache-Control, ETag, and Last-Modified improve web performance?
reference_answer: Cache-Control directives (max-age, public/private, no-cache, immutable) tell browsers and CDNs how long responses can be reused without hitting the origin. ETag and Last-Modified enable conditional requests (If-None-Match / If-Modified-Since), letting the server reply with a lightweight 304 Not Modified when the resource has not changed.
expected_concepts: Cache-Control directives|ETag validator|conditional requests|304 Not Modified|CDN and browser caching

question: Compare Client-Side Rendering (CSR), Server-Side Rendering (SSR), and Static Site Generation (SSG).
reference_answer: CSR ships minimal HTML plus JavaScript that fetches data and renders in the browser, offering snappy client navigation but slower First Contentful Paint and weaker default SEO. SSR renders HTML per request on the server for fast initial paint and dynamic SEO at higher server CPU cost. SSG pre-builds HTML at build time for CDN-speed delivery on content that changes infrequently.
expected_concepts: First Contentful Paint|hydration|SEO crawlability|server compute trade-off|CDN edge caching

question: How would you design API rate limiting and prevent thundering herds under traffic spikes?
reference_answer: Apply token bucket or sliding-window rate limits backed by atomic Redis scripts keyed by user/IP, returning 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After headers. To prevent cache stampedes (thundering herds), use request coalescing (singleflight), jittered TTLs, stale-while-revalidate caching, and exponential backoff on clients.
expected_concepts: token bucket or sliding window|Redis atomic counters|429 Retry-After|cache stampede mitigation|jittered TTL and backoff
